summary: This memo documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocols. It updates and obsoletes RFC 943. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 990.

eli5.summary: A list of agreed numbers for network things, brought up to date. It was soon replaced by a newer list.

questions: where to find assigned numbers in 1985
where to find assigned protocol numbers
subtitle: Updated registry of protocol numbers, addresses, ports, and network identifiers as of December 1985

tldr.problem: Growing Internet requires current registry of all assigned protocol parameter values including network numbers, version numbers, protocol identifiers, port assignments, and hardware type codes.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations, updated from RFC 900 with new assignments and network additions from 1984-1985.
tldr.outcome: Provides the definitive registry for protocol parameter assignments for the mid-1980s Internet. Historic and replaced by RFC 990.

today: RFC 960 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 990 in November 1986. The assigned numbers registry function evolved from centralized RFCs into the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), eventually transitioning to online registries maintained by regional registries and ICANN. Modern protocol parameter assignments use IANA registries maintained in digital form rather than periodic paper RFCs.

sections.title: Introduction and Network Growth
sections.content:
RFC 960 documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations. It is issued in December 1985 and obsoletes RFC 943, RFC 923 (which obsoleted RFC 900), RFC 900, and earlier assigned number RFCs. The RFC will be updated periodically, with assignments handled by Joyce Reynolds at USC-ISI.

The document notes that most protocols are documented in the RFC series, with the more prominent ones in the Internet Protocol Transition Workbook or old ARPANET Protocol Handbook. The assignment of network numbers, protocol types, and port numbers follows the same process as earlier registries, with network administrators contacting Joyce Reynolds for number assignments.
sections.eli5: This is an official updated list from December 1985 saying "here are all the numbers we're using now, including new ones since last year." It's the more recent version of RFC 900.

sections.title: IP Address Classes and Network Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC details the three classes of Internet Protocol addresses. Class A uses a 7-bit network number and 24-bit local address with the highest-order bit set to 0, allowing 128 networks. Class B uses a 14-bit network number and 16-bit local address with bits 1-0 in the high-order positions, allowing 16,384 networks. Class C uses a 21-bit network number and 8-bit local address with bits 1-1-0 in the high-order positions, allowing over 2 million networks.

Network numbers are categorized by user type: Research (R), Defense (D), Government (G), and Commercial (C). The document includes special address conventions: address zero means "this" network, and all-ones addresses mean "all" hosts. Networks are marked with indicators for temporary assignments (T), independent networks (*), and references showing responsible parties.
sections.eli5: Internet addresses come in three sizes for big, medium, and small networks. Each network has a code showing if it's for research, military, government, or business. Some are marked as temporary or independent.

sections.title: Version Numbers, Protocols, and Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC specifies IP version numbers: version 0 and 15 are reserved, versions 1-3 and 6-14 are unassigned, version 4 is the Internet Protocol standard, and version 5 is ST Datagram Mode. Protocol numbers identify the next-level protocol following the IP header. Common protocols include ICMP (1), GGP (3), TCP (6), UDP (17), EGP (8), and many others up to 79, with 80-254 unassigned and 255 reserved.

The RFC includes more protocol numbers than RFC 900, such as EMCON (14), RDP (27), IRTP (28), and ISO-TP4 (29), reflecting the growth of protocol diversity between 1984 and 1985. Autonomous System Numbers from 0 to 65535 are assigned for use with gateway protocols. Other assignments include ARPANET logical addresses, ARPANET link numbers, IEEE 802 Service Access Point codes, and Address Resolution Protocol parameters.
sections.eli5: Different protocols get different numbers. TCP is one, UDP is another. As the network grew, more protocol numbers were assigned. The document includes all the new ones added since 1984.

sections.title: Port Numbers and Service Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC assigns well-known port numbers for network services. Ports are used in TCP to name the ends of logical connections. Common assignments include port 21 for FTP (File Transfer), port 23 for TELNET, port 25 for SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer), port 42 for NAMESERVER, port 53 for DOMAIN (Domain Name Server), port 69 for TFTP, port 79 for FINGER, and port 109 for POP (Post Office Protocol).

The assigned ports follow a convention where all except the low-order eight bits are cleared to zero. The same port assignments are used with UDP where possible. The RFC notes that the well-known port list is reserved for assignment by IANA (though the term IANA is not yet formally used). Higher port numbers (224-241, 243-255) are either unassigned or reserved for experimental use.
sections.eli5: Services listen on numbered doors called ports. Port 21 is FTP, port 23 is Telnet, port 25 is email. These were agreed standard door numbers.

sections.title: Network Types, Hardware Codes, and Other Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC documents Ethernet numbers for protocol identification (such as 0800 for DOD IP and 0600 for XEROX NS IDP), IEEE 802 SAP codes, ARP operation codes and hardware types, ARPANET link assignments, and terminal type names. It includes expanded lists reflecting the growth of heterogeneous network types in use.

Network totals show significant growth from 1984: total networks assigned grew from 902 to 1,608, with increases particularly in Class B and Class C networks. Research networks expanded from 867 to 981 assignments. The RFC also documents the many networks and subnets allocated to commercial vendors and emerging computer companies like Hewlett Packard, Apple Computer, Sun Microsystems, and Symbolics.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of networks used different numbering schemes for messages. Ethernet has its own numbers, 802 networks have theirs. The list shows all of them and how much the network had grown in one year.
